claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is a non-equilibrium, metastable single-phase solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
A diffusional instability governs the evolution of the metastable solid solution.
The diffusional instability drives nucleation and growth of fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form both at grain boundaries and within grains.
The precipitates alter local diffusion pathways and interfacial energies.
Mg has a high chemical potential in the proposed alloy state.
Mg diffuses faster than the heavier alloying elements during aging.
Mg segregates during aging and forms Mg-rich intermetallic compounds from the metastable matrix.
Fine, uniformly distributed Mg-rich precipitates nucleate adherent MgO-containing protective oxide phases.
Oxide nucleation on finely dispersed precipitates produces a continuous protective scale.
A continuous protective scale preserves or improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Fine, dispersed precipitates preserve or improve corrosion resistance.
Coarsened or interconnected intermetallic precipitates interrupt oxide-scale continuity.
Interconnected precipitates create galvanic or stress concentrations.
Galvanic or stress concentrations facilitate oxide spallation and accelerated degradation.
Coarsened or interconnected precipitates lead to higher oxidation rates.
Coarsened or interconnected precipitates lead to increased corrosion current.
Isothermal aging near 750 °C promotes transformation and precipitation relative to rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching suppresses transformation and retains the metastable as-cast state.
The proposed mechanism is operative above approximately 700 °C and in corrosive environments where oxide-scale integrity controls longevity.
